list.q: Where do I start on the history of Bayesian thought?
list.title: Bayes, from the 1763 essay to the working textbook

stops.caption: Start with the story: a narrative history of Bayes' rule from its 18th-century origins to code-breaking and modern computing. It gives you the map before the primary sources.
The seed. Bayes' essay, published posthumously by Richard Price in 1763, asks how to infer an unknown chance from observed frequencies.
Laplace turns inverse probability into a general method and explains it for a lay reader, including his sunrise example. Its year here is estimated from his life dates.
Boole recasts logic as algebra and applies it to probability, and he objects to assuming equal priors when nothing is known.
The frequentist reply: Venn defines probability as a proportion in a long series and rejects inverse probability. This is the third edition.
Jevons keeps the Laplacean line alive, treating scientific induction as inverse probability.
Keynes treats probability as a logical relation between propositions, a bridge from the 19th-century logicians to 20th-century subjectivism.
Jaynes rebuilds probability as extended logic, from Cox's theorem to maximum entropy, in a textbook published after his death.
The standard applied text: hierarchical models, model checking and computation.
A teaching-first course in Bayesian modelling with code, where many practitioners now begin.
